entry.title: The inadequacy of climate action
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The inadequacy of climate actionThe inadequacy of climate action

With the 1.5°C threshold expected to be breached within years, India must pay greater attention to adaptation and resilience

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Nitin Desai6 min read Last Updated : Oct 13 2026 | 11:07 PM ISTSustainable development is defined as meeting the needs of the present without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs.  The threat of climate change, however, requires something more than this. The issue is not just avoiding things today that will worsen climate in the present or the future.  Our actions now have to take into account the established probability of climate worsening for humans in the near future.  That is why the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) was negotiated and ratified a little over three decades ago. Its preamble stated that “responses to climate change should be coordinated with social and economic development in an integrated manner with a view to avoiding adverse impacts on the latter”.  This has not happened. The integration of climate action with development has played a role in the growth of renewable energy, though even here the boom may be attributable more to the improved commercial prospects because of reduced capital costs. The reality is that policymaking for climate action is separated from development policy formulation.  In practice, development needs and profit potentials drive both present and future actions. That is why the performance of the member states of the UNFCCC on climate mitigation are abysmal. An independent organisation, Climate Action Tracker, evaluates the performance of major countries towards the goal of 1.5°C set in the Paris Agreement in 2015. In its assessment, the actions of practically all the major states are insufficient.  The United States, Russia, the Gulf States and much of Southeast Asia are rated as “critically insufficient”; India, China, Egypt, Brazil, Argentina, Canada and Mexico are rated as “highly insufficient”; most of Europe, Australia and South Africa are rated as “insufficient”.  If all countries followed the level of climate action associated with each category, the resulting global temperature rise would be 4°C for the “critically insufficient” category, be 3-4°C for the “highly insufficient”, and be 2-3°C for the “insufficient” category. The issue is not whether the countries will reach what they have promised for 2030. India will and may even exceed the target. The real issue is that the stated targets for 2030 are inadequate for reaching the global limit of 1.50C. The situation now has worsened with the withdrawal of the US from the Paris Agreement and from the UNFCCC, which will take effect in January 2027. Their malign impact will be seen in this year’s meeting of the UNFCCC in Antalya, Türkiye.   Quite frankly we must accept that because of their limited promises, the world will not succeed in limiting future temperature increases to the goals set in the Paris Agreement.  On September 2, the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) published a report recognising for the first time that the 1.5°C threshold will be breached within a matter of years, not decades. Climate policy must now focus as much on building up resilience to higher temperatures and adaptation as on climate change mitigation. This is part of the agenda for the UNFCCC. But the actual design and implementation of resilience and adaptation will differ greatly depending on local conditions. This is what India should now pay greater attention to in its climate policy. Are we doing enough on adaptation and resilience? An index measuring a country’s exposure, sensitivity and capacity to adapt to the negative effects of climate change across six sectors — food, water, health, ecosystem services, human habitat, and infrastructure — places India at level 28 out of 48 in Asia-Pacific.  Its neighbours, other than Sri Lanka, are below this level and even more vulnerable to climate change risks.  In India, we need to raise the importance of a climate change management strategy that connects it more directly with the main framework of development policy. Looking at the long-term trend of development requires proper integration of climate change management with traditional development actions, such as agricultural growth targets and the adaptation of agriculture to rising temperatures, which may go up to 50°C in summer, their impact on health, and the energy demand they will generate for cooling. We must recognise that cooperation between neighbouring countries on interlinked climate-related impacts, such as those affecting shared rivers, may be necessary and useful. The most important planning need is to raise the importance of climate change management by setting up a National Climate Management Body involving the Centre, states, and the municipalities of very large cities to review and evaluate the adequacy of adaptation and mitigation efforts and secure agreement on future plans for climate management. A major reason for this is that the formulation and implementation of adaptation actions and building up resilience have to be at the local level and involve sectors that are well within state control and management.  Since climate action generally aims at future challenges, we must design climate management programmes that deliver more immediate benefits. For example, forest restoration and strengthening can increase carbon sequestration while also improving water supply; renewable energy can improve the availability of local power supplies; and electric vehicles can reduce running costs. Such co-benefits will make long-term actions more acceptable.  While adaptation and resilience management can be led by state governments and local authorities, the continuing drive for climate change mitigation must remain a central responsibility. So far, much of the focus has been on the promotion of renewable energy. But there are now programmes involving compliance standards and carbon pricing. These include the Carbon Credit Trading Scheme, which imposes emission-intensity targets on several energy-intensive industries and allows trading to address surpluses and deficits, and the Environment Audit Rules, 2025, which provide for environmental audits of industries with a potentially adverse impact on climate change, along with a host of other activities.  Placing these under the oversight of the National Climate Management Body suggested above can strengthen pressure for compliance. One must also recognise that carbon capture, utilisation and storage (CCUS) may be a necessity for major carbon-emitting industries such as steel and cement. At present, India’s share of global CCUS activity is negligible, and the Union government must vigorously pursue the five-year provision of ~20,000 crore made in the 2026-27 Budget.  The Centre can play a major role in helping states, not just by providing sufficient finance for their broad-based climate action, but also by using satellite imagery and artificial intelligence to improve information on climate impacts and actions, link climate action with development activities, and improve the effectiveness of climate-related policies and programmes.  I have focused on national action. But we must recognise our continuing need for more effective global cooperation on climate change mitigation and on the provision of technology and finance required for both mitigation and adaptation. Right now, the prospects for effective global cooperation appear bleak. But as the impacts of climate change become more evident — as seen recently in the high temperatures experienced in the northern states — global cooperation may become more effective. Hopefully, we will see some early signs of this at next month’s UNFCCC meeting.

entry.title: The medical poverty trap is real
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / The medical poverty trap is realThe medical poverty trap is real

Beyond universal coverage, India needs health care facilities that deliver timely, reliable and quality care, not merely exist

premium

The households that can least afford expensive medical treatment are often the households most dependent on providers who charge considerably more than public facilities | Image: Bloomberg

Vachaspati ShuklaSantosh Kumar Dash5 min read Last Updated : Oct 13 2026 | 11:15 PM ISTThe latest findings from the National Sample Survey’s 80th Round, covering January-December 2025, raise uncomfortable questions about the accessibility and affordability of medical services in India. The survey highlights two important trends: A substantial rise in reported morbidity across the country and continued reliance on private health care providers. More importantly, treatment at private facilities imposes a significantly higher financial burden on patients than treatment at public hospitals.  Rising morbidity: The proportion of people reporting an ailment during the preceding 15 days increased considerably in the 80th Round compared with the 75th Round (July 2017-June 2018). In rural India, it nearly doubled, rising from 6.8 per cent to 12.2 per cent, while in urban India, it increased from 9.1 per cent to 14.9 per cent. At first glance, this increase might appear entirely negative. However, higher reported morbidity does not necessarily mean that Indians have suddenly become less healthy. It could also reflect an ageing population and greater health awareness, allowing illnesses to be reported more frequently.  Private providers dominate: According to the latest NSS estimates, 65.4 per cent of treated non-hospitalised ailments in rural India were managed by private providers. In urban India, the figure was 74.8 per cent. The state-level differences are particularly noteworthy. In rural Odisha, 60.9 per cent of treated ailments were handled by government-run facilities. Tamil Nadu and Chhattisgarh also recorded public health care utilisation above 50 per cent. By contrast, public health care accounted for only 15.8 per cent of treated ailments in rural Punjab and less than one-fourth in several other states. This tells us that public health care utilisation is not simply a function of income or geography. It is not simply a matter of consumer preference — it is a verdict on availability, waiting times, perceived quality and the uneven reach of public facilities. This has major implications for household finances, as treatment in private hospitals requires substantially higher out-of-pocket expenditure.  Enormous cost difference: For a treated non-hospitalised ailment, the average out-of-pocket expenditure in India was ₹304 in rural government facilities and ₹257 in urban government facilities. The corresponding expenditure at private hospitals was ₹1,541 and ₹1,343. These gaps also vary widely across states. In urban areas, treatment at a government hospital cost ₹47 in Tamil Nadu but ₹830 in Bihar; at a private hospital, it ranged from ₹834 in Kerala to ₹3,509 in Bihar. The cost of falling ill depends not only on the provider but on the state — a second layer of inequality.  High cost of hospitalisation: In-patient treatment is far more punishing. The average out-of-pocket expenditure per hospitalisation, excluding childbirth, was ₹31,484 in rural India and ₹38,688 in urban India. But the average expenditure in private hospitals was ₹47,710 in rural areas and ₹54,999 in urban areas, compared with only ₹6,905 and ₹6,032, respectively, in government hospitals.  A family facing a large medical bill has limited choices. It may borrow money, postpone other essential expenditures, or sell productive assets. For households already living close to the poverty line, a serious illness can, therefore, become an economic shock from which recovery is difficult. This is the so-called medical poverty trap: Illness reduces a household’s economic security, while economic insecurity, in turn, makes it harder to obtain timely and quality health care. This risk is greatest in economically weaker states such as Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, which depend heavily on private care despite lower household incomes.This creates a fundamental policy contradiction. The households that can least afford expensive medical treatment are often the households most dependent on providers who charge considerably more than public facilities.  Insurance is not enough: This is where schemes such as Ayushman Bharat have an important role in improving financial protection. But an insurance card cannot compensate for the absence of a functioning public-health facility nearby. Nor can insurance by itself ensure the availability of medicines, diagnostic services, doctors, and quality primary care. Health care financing and health care delivery must, therefore, be considered together. Health insurance and financing schemes, meanwhile, have expanded. Coverage rose from 14.1 per cent in 2017-18 to 47.4 per cent in 2025 in rural areas; and from 19.1 per cent to 44.3 per cent in urban areas. While this is a substantial change, the reported out-of-pocket medical expenditure remains high. This does not mean that insurance has failed; it means that nominal coverage is not the same as effective financial protection.  Ayushman Bharat and other schemes can reduce catastrophic expenditure only if eligible households know how to use them, if hospitals are available and empanelled, and if covered services match actual needs. The survey’s numbers, therefore, point to a broader problem. India has expanded the architecture of health financing faster than it has repaired the everyday capacity of public care.  Way forward: India needs to strengthen public health care at every level, from Ayushman Arogya Mandirs to district hospitals, so that facilities deliver timely, quality care rather than merely exist. The aim is not to eliminate private health care, but to make the choice between public and private genuine. Universal coverage must mean that seeking treatment does not threaten a family’s economic survival. Absent this, the private sector will remain the default provider and households will remain the default financiers.

entry.title: Are financial risks now building?
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Are financial risks now building?Are financial risks now building?

Financial transactions and risks may be expanding faster than the regulatory perimeter designed to oversee them

premium

Banks today are generally more resilient than they were before 2008. But finance has moved on

Anoop Singh5 min read Last Updated : Oct 12 2026 | 11:09 PM ISTFinancial crises often occur when the architecture designed to safeguard stability fails to keep pace with the changing financial system. New institutions and transactions expand the perimeter of finance while regulation, supervision and crisis-management arrangements adjust more slowly. Risks accumulate where they are poorly measured or understood — until a shock reveals how interconnected they have become.  This was part of the story of earlier crises. The Asian financial crisis exposed vulnerabilities from rapid cross-border flows, foreign-currency borrowing, and weak financial-sector oversight. A decade later, the global financial crisis revealed how securitisation, leverage and shadow banking had developed beyond the reach of an architecture still focused heavily on regulated banks.  Could a similar gap be opening again? Banks today are generally more resilient than they were before 2008. But finance has moved on. Non-bank financial institutions (NBFIs) accounted for 51 per cent of global financial assets in 2024 and grew at twice the pace of banks. At the same time, near-record government debt and the growing role of NBFIs have changed sovereign debt markets, with the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) warning that the combination can heighten the risk of market dysfunction.  Risk has migrated: Post-2008 reforms strengthened banks, but some risks migrated elsewhere. Hedge funds can carry substantial leverage, investment funds face liquidity mismatches, and private credit has expanded rapidly. Yet banks remain connected through credit lines, repo, and derivatives. The relevant unit of analysis is increasingly not the individual bank but a sovereign-bank-NBFI-market network.  Japan provides a striking illustration. Decades of exceptionally low interest rates made the yen a global funding currency. Cross-border yen borrowing reached an estimated ¥360 trillion ($2.3 trillion) by March 2026, an increase of more than two-thirds from its level in late 2021. Yet the true scale of the carry trade remains uncertain because derivatives and off-balance-sheet positions can be difficult for regulators to observe.  As the Bank of Japan normalises monetary policy, a rapid yen appreciation could force leveraged investors to unwind positions elsewhere. The partial unwinding of the yen carry trade in 2024 showed how quickly such pressures can spread: The effects reached Japanese, US, European and other Asian equity markets, cryptocurrencies and emerging-market currencies. Japan illustrates the wider problem —  transactions have become global and interconnected while supervision remains predominantly national.  Is the protective perimeter weakening? This comes as parts of the regulatory architecture face pressure. US Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr has warned that recent regulatory changes have reduced capital requirements for large American banks and that divergence from international standards could encourage a regulatory “race to the bottom”. US bank credit commitments to other financial entities exceeded $2.6 trillion in the second half of 2025. Regulatory simplification extends elsewhere. Proposed US changes would substantially reduce the number of listed companies requiring independent auditor attestation of internal financial controls introduced after the Enron accounting scandal. Compliance costs are a legitimate concern. But companies already exempt from the requirement have accounted for 60-80 per cent of annual financial restatements in recent years.  Technology is simultaneously extending the perimeter. Financial Stability Board Chair Andrew Bailey has warned that frontier artificial intelligence (AI) could expose financial institutions to simultaneous disruption through cyberattacks and shared technology dependencies. Common AI models, automated trading, and dependence on common technology providers could create correlated behaviour or operational failures across otherwise unrelated institutions.  Who can provide the new perimeter? The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and BIS are central to closing these gaps — but neither can itself provide a global regulatory perimeter. The IMF can bring sovereign, macroeconomic and financial risks together through surveillance and financial-sector assessments. The BIS and Basel Committee can develop common prudential standards, identify cross-border risks and encourage consistent supervision. But neither is a supranational regulator. Implementation and enforcement remain national. The answer must, therefore, be a more connected architecture, with national regulators following risks beyond traditional institutional boundaries; international standards limiting regulatory arbitrage; better cross-border information on leverage and liquidity; and IMF surveillance assessing whether the pieces add up to system-wide resilience. The regulatory perimeter increasingly needs to follow the activity and the risk, not simply the institution undertaking it.  India provides an instructive counterpoint. Regulation and supervision have strengthened considerably following earlier banking distress, and the IMF’s latest financial-sector assessment finds banks and nonbanks broadly resilient. Yet India’s financial system is also evolving: Nonbanks now provide nearly half of private-sector credit, while connections among banks, non-banking financial companies and markets have grown. The lesson from India is, therefore, encouraging but also relevant more widely — that regulatory authorities need to continually adapt the perimeter as financial activity, institutions and their interconnections change.  The emerging-market test: This matters particularly for emerging economies. Financial instability need not originate within them. An advanced-economy shock can arrive through portfolio outflows, currency depreciation, higher sovereign yields and refinancing costs. The yen carry trade demonstrates how leveraged positions created elsewhere can suddenly affect emerging-market assets. None of this means another financial crisis is imminent. It suggests something subtler: Financial transactions and risks may once again be expanding faster than the perimeter designed to oversee them. The next crisis may look nothing like 1997 or 2008. The more important question is whether the financial architecture has evolved sufficiently to see it coming — and to contain it when it does.

entry.title: Maximising value, not the haircut
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Maximising value, not the haircutMaximising value, not the haircut

Creditors must look beyond immediate recovery to the future value a resolution plan can create

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

M S SahooSanjeev Pandey6 min read Last Updated : Oct 12 2026 | 10:43 PM ISTThe Supreme Court has described the Committee of Creditors (CoC) as the protagonist of insolvency resolution under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code (IBC), 2016. It decides the fate of a distressed corporate debtor (CD) — whether it should be rescued through a resolution plan or sent into liquidation. Whichever course it chooses, the objective is to resolve the stress while maximising the value of the assets of the CD.  The decision is commercial and ordinarily beyond judicial substitution. It is not amenable to arithmetic. A plan with the highest evaluation score, net present value, or upfront payment does not, by itself, determine the outcome. The decision rests on voting informed by commercial wisdom.  The IBC does not use the expression “commercial wisdom”. It is, however, now firmly embedded in IBC jurisprudence to describe a well-considered decision directed towards the statutory objective of maximising the value of the CD, though the CoC often seeks to maximise the outcome for creditors. These two forms of maximisation are not synonymous, though they are aligned to a large extent.  Creditors hold claims against the CD, ultimately linked to the value of the enterprise and its assets. If the CD is rescued, restored to health and made more productive, the pool from which creditors can derive value increases. Maximising the value of the CD should, therefore, maximise the value available to creditors.  The difference arises from the time horizon and the structure of the resolution plan. Creditors may remain economically connected with the enterprise through equity, continued credit, deferred or contingent consideration, or other arrangements. If they retain an interest in the future of the CD and the enterprise prospers, maximising the CD’s value and maximising their own value move together.  The position differs when creditors take their recovery upfront and walk away. They exit when the enterprise is at its weakest, exchanging participation in the future value for immediate realisation. Once they exit, they have little “skin in the game” in its post-resolution value creation. In choosing immediate recovery, they may compromise the future value of the CD and consequently their own value.  That distinguishes recovery and resolution.  Recovery asks: What can be obtained from the enterprise in its present condition? Resolution asks: What can the enterprise become if its distress is addressed? They have different economic implications.  Recovery focuses primarily on distributing the value presently available. Resolution plan, by contrast, seeks to preserve a viable enterprise and create conditions for future value. A successful resolution can keep productive assets in use, preserve relationships with employees, suppliers and customers, attract fresh capital, change management or strategy, and address the causes of distress. Instead of distributing existing value, it enables the enterprise to create more.  This is why a resolution applicant is willing to invest. It sees value not merely in what remains, but in what can be created. Creditors should consider not only what they can obtain from the CD today, but what the enterprise can become tomorrow. If they remain economically connected with the enterprise, they can participate not only in the value preserved through the resolution plan but also in the additional value created by its revival.  Evidence from post-resolution outcomes shows that companies do revive and prosper. Operations can improve, capacity can be better utilised, customers can return, fresh capital can be invested and enterprise value can increase. A creditor that has taken an upfront settlement and completely exited does not participate in that subsequent increase. It may, in effect, have left the gains from revival to the acquirer. This does not mean that creditors should always accept a lower upfront payment or always take equity. Nor should uncertain future returns automatically be preferred to certain present value. Time, risk, probability of success and certainty of payment are legitimate commercial considerations. But future value is not irrelevant because creditors have the power to take money out today.  There is a legitimate institutional reason why banks tend to prefer cash. Cash can be booked, provided for, and closed. Equity requires valuation, monitoring, patience, and eventual monetisation. A banker who accepts less cash today in return for equity tomorrow may have to justify that decision years later if the turnaround fails. A defensible immediate recovery can, therefore, appear safer than a potentially larger one in future. Yet the rush to realise dues upfront sits uneasily with the very reason financial creditors have been entrusted with the central role in insolvency resolution: Their ability to wait and realise their dues from the improved performance of a revived corporate debtor.  The challenge is to make value-maximising decisions defensible. CoCs could, for example, invite bids in both all-cash and cash-plus-upside formats and compare them on a properly risk-adjusted basis. Regulators could provide a clear framework for valuing and accounting for equity or contingent consideration received under an approved resolution plan. A reasoned decision to retain an interest in future value, supported by due diligence and documented assumptions about risk and probability, should be recognised as legitimate commercial judgement rather than treated with hindsight as imprudence.  This would distinguish between accepting uncertain value because it is genuinely superior after adjusting for risk, and accepting cash simply because it is easier to justify. The first is commercial wisdom. The second may be institutional risk aversion masquerading as commercial wisdom.  A resolution plan should, therefore, be judged not only by what creditors receive when it is approved, but also by what it enables thereafter: Whether the business survives, whether productive assets remain productive, whether fresh investment comes in, whether financial and operational weaknesses are repaired, and whether the enterprise is capable of creating value beyond the point at which it entered insolvency.  The CoC has a responsibility to exercise commercial wisdom consistently with the statutory objective. Maximising the value of the CD should maximise the value available to creditors. But when creditors choose to exit at the point of maximum distress, they may maximise neither the value of the CD nor their own value. They may simply be maximising their haircut.  
  The writers are, respectively, emeritus fellow, Insolvency Law Academy, and an insolvency professional and consultant   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Four reforms to enhance trust in insurance sector
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Four reforms to enhance trust in insurance sectorFour reforms to enhance trust in insurance sector

From commission-free insurance plans to fee-only advisers and public complaint records, four reforms could improve transparency, curb mis-selling and help policyholders make informed choices

premium

As Irdai considers changes to insurance distribution, four proposals could strengthen consumer protection

Harsh Roongta4 min read Last Updated : Oct 11 2026 | 11:49 PM IST“The man who announces and pauses tariffs on the same day”, “The most mis-sold product in India” and “Claim denied”. All readers will recognise the person in the first phrase. Similarly, it is a shame that mis-selling immediately brings life insurance to mind, and claim denial, health insurance.  That distrust is damaging because insurance helps households recover financially from death, disability, illness or natural and man-made calamities. It is the bedrock of any sound financial plan. The life insurance industry’s advertisement “Sabse pehle Insurance” (insurance before anything else, including investments) is absolutely right for pure protection insurance.  The Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India (Irdai) acknowledges several reasons for this distrust in its path-breaking consultation paper on distribution reforms. “Interests of insurers, distributors and public are misaligned. ... However, prevailing remuneration structures place greater emphasis on premium procurement rather than suitability or persistency or long-term customer outcomes.” “Sales are commission led instead of pricing and quality led.” “High cost and uncertain service quality is weakening trust and limiting coverage.” These are the restrained words of the industry regulator, not an industry critic.   The paper rightly calls distribution reforms a “compelling priority”. They include bringing back commission limits and gradually lowering the expenses insurers can charge policyholders. The paper also seeks to simplify how insurance is sold, set up Bima Sugam as a not-for-profit insurance marketplace, and promote informational transparency through a Public Insurance Registry (PIR).   Predictably, industry players have protested. They seek to protect the status quo, especially on distribution commissions. They argue that the reforms will affect the employment of lakhs of agents. That argument does not wash. Employment cannot justify misleading and exploiting millions of fellow citizens.  The Irdai chairman has said that the voice of the public is missing when insurance regulations are made. The industry is heard well. Policyholders are not. This column will try to fill that gap. Here are four suggestions to put policyholders first, even if industry pressure stalls the commission reforms.   First, change the measure of success. The job of insurance is to protect. Yet the insurance industry measures penetration as the premium collected as a percentage of GDP. This is like measuring progress on a journey by the amount paid for petrol instead of the distance covered. If petrol becomes expensive, it cannot be celebrated as progress. Measure the protection amount per person instead. That would refocus the industry on its core function.  Second, launch Bima Sugam without further delay. It should offer simple term and health insurance products at prices with no commission built in. This would let consumers compare prices and decide whether an agent’s service is worth the extra cost. The “direct” plan model in mutual funds is a useful parallel. Direct plans now account for about 45 per cent of mutual fund assets, just 13 years after their introduction. These have helped moderate commissions by bringing in transparency and competition. Bima Sugam can do the same for insurance.  Third, allow fee-only insurance advisers, much like investment advisers in the securities market. Paid by clients alone, these advisers would receive no commissions from insurers. They would have a duty to put their clients’ interests first. This would give consumers access to independent advice on the insurance they need.  Fourth, add complaint records and the decisions on them to the proposed Public Insurance Registry. Consumers should be able to check these easily before choosing an insurer or intermediary. It would be especially useful in health insurance, where claim denial is routine. It would help consumers make better choices until Irdai brings suitable reforms for that sector.  Truth be told, the tariff man may dominate the headlines for the next few years. However, the immediate association of life insurance with “mis-selling” and health insurance with “claim denied” will take much longer to fade. Trust will come as policyholders see claims paid and policies sold honestly. Irdai’s reforms, together with these suggestions, can begin that process. Only when the industry earns that trust can “Insurance liya accha kiya” mean what it says. ____________________________________________________________________________________________________  The writer heads Fee-Only Investment Advisors LLP, a Sebi-registered investment advisor; X (formerly Twitter): @harshroongta   Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Himalayan blunders and beyond
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Himalayan blunders and beyondHimalayan blunders and beyond

There is no getting away from the historical responsibility of the richest and most developed countries for this loss of lives

premium

We know that the climate-change ticking bomb has been exacerbated by the “nature” of development in these ecological hotspots (Photo: Wikimedia Commons)

Sunita Narain5 min read Last Updated : Oct 11 2026 | 10:44 PM ISTAs I write this, over 1,410 lives have been confirmed lost and many thousands are still missing in the floods in Nepal, as the mighty Himalayas came down as rubble. This is an enormous and painful human tragedy, but it is also about wilful actions and inactions of humans. This tragedy is really about our mindset, the belief that we, as humans, can re-engineer everything; that we are in control of the universe and all things in it. We are the supreme beings who can weather climate change, because, after all, it is only about a small and insignificant matter of weather. This is on us.  Let me break this down. First comes the question of what happened in Nepal on August 26. The images that all of us would have seen are of the mountain coming down — just collapsing — as the flash flood and massive quantity of debris buried everything in its path, taking with it the huge building of the Chinese immigration office. It is a frightening visual, straight out of a science-fiction movie. We know now that this flash flood was not caused by an extreme cloudburst. It was triggered by the collapse of a high-altitude glacier near the Langtang Lirung peak. An estimated 142 million cubic metres of ice and rocks were dislodged, creating a 5.2 magnitude seismic event. This then led to the formation of natural dams, behind which water and moraine accumulated, and when the dams broke, they unleashed even more devastating floods downstream.  The second question is: Why? There is no single headline reason, but two events have greatly contributed to this and other such tragedies in this region. One is the well-documented warming caused by climate change. It is literally weakening the Himalayas — the temperature rise melts glaciers; this, in turn, corrodes the moraine slopes. It is a ticking bomb, which implodes as it did in Nepal. In addition, climate change is leading to an increased frequency and intensity of extreme weather events, which, in turn, bring flood and landslide catastrophes, like those seen in Himachal Pradesh in 2025, in Sikkim in 2024, and in Chamoli in 2021.  We are complicit in this; all of us, but particularly the countries that have contributed the most to the stock of greenhouse emission in the atmosphere, which, in turn, is driving up temperatures and causing runaway devastations. This is about the past, the present and the future. There is no getting away from the historical responsibility of the richest and most developed countries for this loss of lives. And even as the death toll was rising in Nepal, we got the news that the world was no longer even on an illusionary track to stay below the guardrail of 1.5° Celsius temperature rise since the industrial period of 1870. The United Nations Environment Programme estimates that the world will overshoot this threshold within a few years. Scientists know that beyond 1.5° Celsius, the impacts would be cascading and even more devastating — from the collapse of ice sheets to disruption in ocean currents like the Atlantic Meridional Overtaking Circulation (AMOC), and much more. The intense heat, fires and other weather abnormalities we saw this summer were only a preview of what awaits us. Yet, we seem to be sanguine about this breakdown in our Earth’s system. Today, we are so distracted by economic and livelihood concerns brought on by deliberate human misdeeds like senseless wars that this enormous and existential crisis seems distant and insignificant. We are merely tinkering with emission, not transforming it to live within nature’s bounds.  Let’s get back to the Himalayas. We know that the climate-change ticking bomb has been exacerbated by the “nature” of development in these ecological hotspots. We talk ad nauseam about adaptation and about how we must take the changing climate into account, but we never do. We really believe that we can continue to do what we do, without consequences. Take, for example, the hydroelectric projects being constructed by damming narrow rivers. As I have said in the past, and will repeat it, this is not about dam development but about the recklessness with which they are being developed. In the Indian Himalayas, project after project is coming up — literally back-to-back — so that the Ganga is re-engineered. It will cease to flow naturally because these projects will regulate its water, taking it to generate electricity and then releasing it back. Then we are tunnelling into the mountains and building roads, often without provision for slope management.I can go on.  But the fact is we are not hearing the message that nature is giving us, loud and clear: Change your mindset; your thinking that you can dominate me and bring me to my knees will not work. “Change or perish” is the message. The question is if we can hear it amid the cacophony of our distractions.

entry.title: Consequences of cheap electricity
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Consequences of cheap electricityConsequences of cheap electricity

Opportunities are opening up in energy-intensive sectors

premium

The emerging Indian electrostate calls for a rethink of strategy in private firms | Illustration: Ajaya Mohanty

Ajay Shah5 min read Last Updated : Oct 11 2026 | 10:41 PM ISTIn India, we have a gloomy view of energy costs. Indian coal is of poor quality. Moving it across the country is expensive. For petroleum and gas, domestic prices largely track world prices. The electricity system often socks commercial buyers. The net result is a high-cost energy landscape. Indian firms navigate arbitrary state power, fragile infrastructure, and expensive inputs, including energy. The dominant strategy for successful Indian enterprises was to harness top-decile intellectual capital, to compensate for the three handicaps. This allowed Indian firms to compete in the global economy, primarily in services and asset-light models, to great effect.   A sea change in energy prices is dismantling this old worldview. For the first time, India is emerging as a favourable location for energy costs. Recent research by Nikit Abhyankar and Amol Phadke at the University of California Berkeley (https://bit.ly/ieccucb) brings remarkable facts to light. The capital expenditure required for a solar plant in India is now approximately one-third that in the United States (US). This difference stems from three factors: Interconnection delays, labour costs, and land acquisition. India suffers a penalty on the cost of capital, reflecting the failures of financial economic policy, including capital controls. Overall, the advantages in physical execution outweigh the financial penalty.  Consider solar electricity delivered during daylight hours. In India, this stands at $30 per megawatt-hour (Mwh) whereas the US price is closer to $50 per Mwh. For firm power, where solar is bundled with battery storage to provide round-the-clock energy, this is $70 per Mwh in India compared to $100 per Mwh in the US.  The US was the original fossil-fuel hegemon. It built its economic supremacy upon the combustion of wood, coal, oil, and gas. Research funding by the US government made the renewables revolution. The traditional view held that competing with the US on energy costs was impossible. But the emerging Indian electrostate is now delivering a powerful new Indian macro-fundamental. There are, of course, countries that beat India on energy costs. But surpassing the US is a big thing. Now, producing in India has two distinct advantages over the US: Cheap labour and cheap energy.  The emerging Indian electrostate calls for a rethink of strategy in private firms. The current structure of Indian industry is based on compensating for expensive energy. The trade liberalisation of 1991-2007 forced firms to find competitive niches. Because energy was expensive, Indian firms favoured business areas that had low energy-intensity. We see this in the Centre for Monitoring Indian Economy (CMIE) database (https://bit.ly/3WieMrA). In 1992-93, power-fuel-water for non-financial firms was 5.73 per cent of expenses. In 2024-25, this had dropped to just 2.87 per cent. But green power now reshapes the frontier of what can be profitably done in India.  Consider the steel industry. Almost all existing steel capacity relies on coal as the primary raw material and energy source. The technological alternative is the production of green steel. This involves using electricity to produce hydrogen, running a direct reduced iron (DRI) shaft furnace to create sponge iron, and melting this iron into steel using an electric arc furnace (EAF). These calculations look good with green hydrogen today in a way that was not the case just a few years ago. Solar and battery electricity is a locked-in nominal rupee price for 25 years while coal prices will rise in the future. As a consequence, green steel is now at rough parity with coal-based steel in India. When exporting to the European Union and the United Kingdom, green steel is superior owing to their Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM).  This technological dislocation presents a unique opportunity for the Indian steel industry. In China, the industrial base is dominated by a billion tonnes/annum fossil-fuel steel capacity. India has the opportunity to build green-steel capacity that can beat this industry. There is a scenario where the billion tonnes/annum Chinese industry becomes a stranded legacy asset, and the Chinese non-market economy will struggle with its bankruptcy. Making aluminium requires electricity and not coal as raw material. As with steel, we get to estimates for green aluminium that are competitive against coal-based production, with an edge when exporting into CBAM countries, once we take into account contemporary prices for green power in India and the locked-in nominal prices for 25 years.  We are at a tipping point in 2026, when these calculations have reached rough parity. From here, the dominance of green technologies will go up through three certainties and two pieces of optimism about India: (a) More countries will adopt the CBAM; (b) progress on solar energy and batteries will continue, and the cost of green power will keep dropping; (c) coal prices will go up with inflation; (d) if Indian macro/finance policy reforms make progress, capital controls will be removed, which will reduce the cost of capital, and then the cost of green power will go down; (e) if the Indian state takes global warming and air quality more seriously, taxes and other restrictions on coal will come.  Boardrooms and investment committees must now rethink strategy in many respects. There are novel investment opportunities in energy-intensive industries in the Indian electrostate. The tail risk of stranded fossil-fuel assets in areas such as electricity, steel and aluminium has gone up. There is a lot at stake. According to the CMIE CapEx database, projects under implementation for primary steel total ₹6.4 trillion, representing roughly 149 million tonnes per annum of capacity. For primary aluminium, projects under implementation total ₹2.6 trillion, representing about 5.8 million tonnes per annum. A good chunk of the aluminium projects is a ₹0.8 trillion bet on new coal-power plants, which is odd by global standards. What is needed in this field is not practitioner knowledge about how the business worked in the last decade but a strategic sense about how the world will change in the next decade. 
 The writer is a researcher at XKDR Forum     Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. They do not necessarily reflect the opinion of www.business-standard.com or the Business Standard newspaperTopics : electricity sector BS Opinion renewable enrgy electricity for all Electricity prices

entry.title: Exim Matters: GST reforms overlook exporters' credit plight
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Exim Matters: GST reforms overlook exporters' credit plightExim Matters: GST reforms overlook exporters' credit plight

Exporters seek a reassessment mechanism or explicit ITC eligibility for IGST paid through ICEGATE challans to regularise AA and EPCG defaults

premium

Goods and Services Tax (GST) reforms aim to simplify compliance, widen input tax credit eligibility and speed up refunds.

TNC Rajagopalan Mumbai 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 11 2026 | 9:56 PM ISTThe Goods and Services Tax (GST) council’s recommendations made last week are welcome, but much of what is presented as next-generation reform amounts to removing longstanding irritants and correcting restrictions that should not have been built into the system. Wider input tax credit (ITC) eligibility, easier registration, faster refunds, and less coercive enforcement will help businesses. Much of this is overdue correction rather than transformation. A lot depends on legal formulations and implementation.  For exporters, obtaining ITC of integrated GST (IGST) paid through challans on the ICEGATE (Indian Customs Electronic Data Interchange Gateway) portal while regularising defaults under Advance Authorisation (AA) and Export Promotion Capital Goods (EPCG) schemes remains an unresolved issue. Here, the government gets the tax, but credit remains uncertain because the challan is not recognised as a document for taking ITC. When an AA holder fails to fulfil export obligation (EO), Para 4.49 of the Handbook of Procedures (HBP) allows regularisation by payment of customs duty on the value of unutilised imported or indigenously procured material under AA plus applicable interest. Paragraph 4.50 prescribes payment through the ICEGATE portal. For EPCG, paragraph 5.21 of HBP provides for payment of duties proportional to the EO shortfall.  The difficulty arises where IGST is paid through a challan without reassessment of the original bill of entry. The additional payment is not automatically reflected in GSTR-2A or GSTR-2B statements. Rule 36(1)(d) of the CGST rules recognises a bill of entry or a similar document prescribed under customs law for assessment of import IGST, but not a payment challan.  In the Becton Dickinson India Private Limited case, the Tamil Nadu advance ruling authority declined ITC against differential import IGST paid through challans following a valuation adjustment. The appellate authority upheld that conclusion on October 8, 2025. Although the case did not concern AA or EPCG default, it illustrates the documentary obstacle. Exporters claiming such ITC through GSTR-3B risk disputes over its admissibility.  A solution, however, is possible. Following the Supreme Court’s judgment in Union of India versus Cosmo Films Limited, CBIC Circular 16/2023-Customs dated June 7, 2023, provided a bill of entry reassessment procedure for regularising violation of the pre-import condition under AA. There is no comparable general procedure for reassessment when other AA or EPCG defaults are regularised. Exporters need a similar workable mechanism or express recognition of challans as documents supporting credit.  Domestic procurement exposes a further complication. An authorisation holder obtaining supplies against an invalidation letter has no bill of entry for those supplies. For EPCG, paragraph 5.21 expressly requires regularisation payments on notional Customs duties, taxes and cess saved on the Free On Rail value of supplies. A challan for such payment cannot refer to an underlying bill of entry because the procurement is from domestic sources. Here, the rules must clarify both the eligibility for credit of the IGST component and the document supporting that credit.  Exporters want to pay and regularise defaults under AA and EPCG authorisations. They need certainty about credit for the IGST they pay. The Council should recommend a general bill of entry reassessment procedure or express provisions recognising ITC eligibility against IGST paid through challans generated through the ICEGATE portal. That would reduce disputes and make regularisation more predictable for exporters. A payment mechanism without credit certainty remains incomplete. Accepting the tax while leaving the credit in doubt is an anomaly that deserves correction.        Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: AI is powering telecom, not just satellites
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / AI is powering telecom, not just satellitesAI is powering telecom, not just satellites

While satellite connectivity makes headlines, agentic AI is quietly transforming telecom into intelligent, self-healing networks

premium

Pranjal Sharma3 min read Last Updated : Oct 11 2026 | 9:09 PM ISTBillionaire technology tycoon Elon Musk is emphatically positioning satellite communications as the answer to connectivity challenges in India and other large markets. The communications industry thinks otherwise, arguing that the choice is not satellite, broadband or mobile connectivity, since each is important. The industry’s true hero is artificial intelligence (AI) in its various emerging versions. Agentic AI is enhancing connections in the era of constant communication.   Despite Musk’s pitch for Starlink in India, the government is unlikely to surrender communications sovereignty. Satellite is among the many options for communications and not the only solution for connecting India. The game-changer is using AI in telecom for affordable and accessible connectivity.  Telecom operators are using smart technologies to enhance affordable services. Agentic AI analyses infrastructure data to predict equipment failure and reduce downtime and maintenance costs. Real-time monitoring of network activity allows AI agents to detect and prevent fraudulent activities, protecting both the company and customers.   AI agents are also being used to independently monitor networks, analyse real-time conditions, make decisions and execute corrective actions with minimal human intervention. This is accelerating the development of self-optimising and self-healing networks that can predict congestion, reroute traffic, allocate resources dynamically, identify faults and improve service while reducing costs. Swedish telecoms equipment maker Ericsson, Indian information technology (IT) giant Infosys and other companies view agentic AI as critical for autonomous network operations.  Agentic AI enables telecom companies to fuse different functions into a single operation. Companies combine connectivity, authentication, cybersecurity and AI-powered automation into integrated solutions for institutional customers. Cisco’s AgenticOps uses AI agents to monitor networks, detect anomalies, correlate telemetry data across infrastructure, diagnose root causes, and in some cases automatically remediate issues. AgenticOps can help IT teams in troubleshooting, configuration management, software updates, branch deployments and network optimisation.  “Agentic AI traffic is a fraction of overall mobile broadband volume today, but it is growing at a rate that makes its future network impact unpredictable. The shift from centralised AI models to distributed autonomous agents will place fundamentally different demands on uplink capacity and latency,” says Erik Ekudden, chief technology officer of Ericsson.   Telecom is shifting from pure connectivity expansion to AI-native, software-defined and satellite-extended intelligent infrastructure. A report by StartUs Insights says that various versions of AI are being adopted by telecom operators. “With 2.25 billion 5G connections, 90 per cent AI adoption among operators, and internet-of-things links heading toward 6.2 billion by 2030, networks are evolving from connectivity pipes into intelligent digital infrastructure,” the report says. Network complexity and operational demands are driving the adoption of AI in telecom automation. Operators face growing pressure to manage dynamic networks while lowering costs. AI-powered automation reduces operational expenses by 30 per cent and improves network efficiency by 25 per cent, the report says.   While deployments remain at varying stages of maturity, Indian telcos such as Bharti Airtel, Reliance Jio, BSNL and Vodafone Idea are using AI-driven systems that can autonomously analyse data, make decisions and execute actions across network operations, customer service and enterprise solutions. Bharti Airtel is using AI for customer experience and enterprise communications. Jio uses AI and machine learning to automate network planning and troubleshooting. BSNL is developing proprietary telecom-focused small language models that can automatically highlight areas with performance degradation.  India’s use of AI for communications can help it develop better capacity and capability even as domestic companies set up sovereign satellite connectivity.

entry.title: Human rights restored
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Human rights restoredHuman rights restored

Navi Pillay is a deserving Nobel Peace Prize winner

premium

Navi Pillay’s decades-long work in human rights law, gender justice and international accountability has shaped the global human rights discourse (Photo:PTI)

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 13 2026 | 10:59 PM ISTIn an ideologically fractured world, the award of the Nobel Peace Prize often attracts controversy. Last year, for instance, the award to a Venezuelan Opposition leader, the right-wing Maria Corina Machado, met with substantial reservations from global liberal establishments. The reservations were confirmed when she gave her medal to United States (US) President Donald Trump after he had invaded her country and captured its President. Mr Trump, of course, thinks he was due to receive the “Noble Prize”, as he termed it, for “stopping eight wars” — though his machinations in West Asia have sent the region and the global economy into turmoil for the foreseeable future. But, barring Mr Trump and the Israeli ruling establishment, few people would quibble with this year’s winner, South Africa’s Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, 85, human rights jurist extraordinaire.  Ms Pillay heard she had got the award when the citation was read in Norway, and her response reveals a wry sense of humour. At  the Nuremberg Palace of Justice — where the first Holocaust trials were held —  she initially thought it was a joke and then told those who had gathered to applaud her that she might share the prize with Mr Trump if they clapped a little harder. But the gravity of the issue for which Ms Pillay won the award is not in doubt. It comes at a time when the world is facing more war and conflict than it has seen in a long time and when the bastion of democratic freedom, the US, is committing human rights violations on its own soil. Ms Pillay’s sterling contribution to shaping the multidimensional facets of human rights law deserves the highest recognition. Most recently (2021-25), she chaired the United Nations (UN) independent enquiry commission on Occupied Palestinian Territory, which accused Israel of committing genocide in Gaza. This finding contradicted entrenched Western assumptions (and tacit approval) of Israel’s actions and marked the first official recognition of Israel’s disproportionate response, especially in targeting Palestinian children, following the Hamas massacre of October 7, 2023.  Ms Pillay, granddaughter of Indian indentured labourers, is the fifth South African to win the Nobel Peace Prize. She shares the honours with Albert Luthuli, Desmond Tutu, Nelson Mandela and F W de Klerk. Apartheid was the leitmotif on which she built her work as a human rights champion. She was the only non-white woman to open her own law practice in Natal province, principally because no law firm wanted its white employees to take instructions from a woman of colour. As a lawyer, she defended several apartheid detainees, including Nelson Mandela, and exposed the use of torture against them. Ms Pillay later graduated from Harvard Law School and became a high court judge after the African National Congress came to power. Her work in the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda brought women’s rights front and centre of human rights debate for the first time by recognising that rape and sexual assault could constitute acts of genocide. Her subsequent work on gender justice at the International Criminal Court — which, ironically, India does not recognise — and focus on caste discrimination as UN Human Rights Commissioner (2008-14) added new dimensions to the issue. By recognising Ms Pillay, who serves as an ad hoc judge at the International Court of Justice in the genocide case against Myanmar over its treatment of the Rohingyas, the Nobel committee has delivered a much-needed restorative to the primacy of human rights in the global discourse.     Topics : Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment nobel peace prize Human Rights South Africa

entry.title: Global growth resilience
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Global growth resilienceGlobal growth resilience

Headline numbers mask vulnerabilities

premium

According to the IMF’s latest assessment, the global economy is expected to grow at 3.1 per cent in 2026, 10 basis points higher than the July update

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 13 2026 | 10:48 PM ISTThe October edition of the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF’s) World Economic Outlook (WEO), released on Tuesday, underscores the broad resilience of the global economy. Despite several disruptions over the past few years, economic growth has broadly held. India has exhibited strong growth performance. According to the IMF’s latest assessment, the global economy is expected to grow at 3.1 per cent in 2026, 10 basis points higher than the July update. Growth is expected to increase to 3.4 per cent in 2027. The IMF has increased India’s growth projection for the current year to 7 per cent, as against its July estimate of 6.4 per cent. Growth in the next financial year too is expected to be 7 per cent, 30 basis points higher than the IMF’s July projection. The upward revision, among other things, is based on resilient domestic demand.  As the WEO explains, two sets of factors have helped the global economy withstand the latest price shocks in energy and commodities. The first is the rerouting of energy supplies, which has meant higher energy production in other countries. Inventory drawdown in many countries also helped. Further, substitution through other sources such as renewables has helped reduce the impact. The second factor is sustained investment in artificial intelligence (AI) and related areas, which has given a significant boost to global economic activities and trade. However, it is worth noting that these factors have limits. If energy supplies from West Asia are not restored quickly, falling inventories could soon get reflected in prices and availability. Further, the AI boom and the lofty valuations of related companies are already raising concerns. If these companies fail to meet expectations, there could be severe disruption in financial markets.  Besides, as the IMF has highlighted, growth is concentrating in a select few countries. Notably, only 32 economies now account for 95 per cent of global growth. This level of growth was spread among 54 economies as recently as April. The percentage of countries with downgraded growth projections has also increased. Thus, growth is being reallocated across countries, depending on their exposure to AI and their ability to deal with war-related supply shocks. The concentration of growth in a few countries, largely driven by an investment boom in a single sector, could pose significant risks to global growth and macroeconomic stability. It is also important to keep in mind that this is happening against the backdrop of elevated public debt, particularly in advanced economies, which is, in part, pushing up interest rates. Tight global financial conditions, owing to large borrowing requirements of governments in advanced economies and the substantial investment needs of AI companies, could affect capital flows to small and emerging-market economies, impacting their growth prospects. It could also increase risks to financial stability.  What does all this mean for India? It is expected to grow at a healthy pace, which the IMF’s projections and revisions have acknowledged. However, it must be noted that India is significantly exposed to disruption in energy supplies and is not a significant beneficiary of the AI boom. In fact, the AI boom elsewhere is partly affecting capital flows, which is impacting both its stock and currency markets. India raised a substantial sum of foreign currency, mainly through non-resident bank deposits, to bolster its reserves to deal with pressures on the balance of payments. However, as recent central-bank intervention in the foreign-currency derivatives market suggests, it has not fundamentally changed the dynamics. Thus, sustaining growth and maintaining macroeconomic stability will require considerable policy agility.     Topics : Business Standard Editorial Comment Editorial Comment IMF growth India GDP

entry.title: A Nobel for shocks
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / A Nobel for shocksA Nobel for shocks

Models of macro management are being tested

premium

Robert E Hall (left) and Michael Woodford(right). Image: X@NobelPrize

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 12 2026 | 10:38 PM ISTThis year’s Nobel Prize in economics has gone to Robert E Hall and Michael Woodford, of Stanford and Columbia Universities, respectively. They are prominent members of the New Keynesian field in macroeconomics, which studies how macroeconomic dynamics — inflation, for example — can be understood in the real structure of the economy. In particular, they have contributed to the study of stabilisation — how central banks and governments can respond to various economic fluctuations, such as business cycles and shocks.  As with almost all recent Nobel Prizes in economics, the timing of the award is part of the story. The field of work for which Professors Hall and Woodford are being honoured emerged in the 1970s, a time when the rise in oil prices challenged economic theory, launched stagflation across the world, and caused great public discontent. In recognising the impact of the work that responded to that moment of disorder — launching, in part, the decades of moderation that followed — the Nobel committee is implicitly throwing out a challenge to those who work on macroeconomics today. Is it possible, perhaps, that these ongoing moments of disruption — the return of economic nationalism, geopolitical shocks to fuel and food prices, the increasing concern that chokepoints could squeeze trade — might produce the next great advances in stabilisation theory.  It should be noted that many of the assumptions on which Professors Woodford and Hall worked — or, perhaps, helped create a consensus around — are themselves being challenged. The notion that an independent central bank can be charged with stabilising the economy, and that this should be taken out of the executive’s hands, is a relatively recent phenomenon — and one that responds to the experience of the 1970s and the theoretical work that grew out of it. But independence can no longer be taken as a given. The President of the United States (US), for example, has clearly sought to bring the US Federal Reserve to heel. Over in Europe, the leading leftist candidate for the French presidency has threatened to jail the head of its central bank for treason.  Broader questions must also be asked about the very nature of “stabilisation”. It often presupposes that shocks are temporary, or that perturbations are part of a business cycle, and that some normal equilibrium can be returned to. But what if the shocks are not transitional? How should macroeconomic stabilisation work under such circumstances? The oil-price shock itself, it should be recalled, was never really reversed; prices settled at a new, permanently higher level. But what if the new normal is not a stable higher price — but erratic, with an upward trend? And how can theory respond to the shifts inherent in the energy transition — or the even greater possible impacts of the technological transition that the growth of artificial intelligence might bring in its wake?  Even if these answers are not immediately available, what should be clear is that the age of Neo-Keynesianism, one in which technocrats could use a well-defined toolbox to deal with relatively predictable peaks and troughs, is past. The global economy is facing stresses greater than any it has seen since the Second World War; and macroeconomic tools and the theory that informs them have to be transformed to match the moment. What is important, however, is that this transformation be grounded in a sensible understanding of the microeconomics of production, consumption, and investment. This, in the end, was what Professors Woodford and Hall contributed, and that insight is timeless.   Topics : Nobel Prize in Economics BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Crude Oil Price

entry.title: Defending the rupee
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / Defending the rupeeDefending the rupee

Govt must act to contain BoP pressure

premium

The RBI's restrictions on forex derivatives and special window for oil marketing companies may ease pressure on the rupee temporarily, but trade and investment reforms remain crucial for long-term currency stability| Representative Picture

Business Standard Editorial Comment3 min read Last Updated : Oct 12 2026 | 10:35 PM ISTThe Reserve Bank of India (RBI) late last week announced a range of measures to support the rupee. As a result, the currency appreciated against the dollar on Monday. The measures included restricting the rebooking of cancelled foreign-exchange derivative contracts involving the rupee for both deliverable and non-deliverable contracts. It also lowered the threshold for undertaking foreign-exchange transactions involving derivatives without establishing an underlying exposure to $5 million from $100 million across all dealers. Further, authorised dealers have to maintain cash with the RBI equivalent to 20 per cent of the rupee value for each foreign-exchange derivative contract involving the rupee with a notional value exceeding $2 million. Besides, the RBI decided to open a special window to address the foreign-exchange needs of the three public-sector oil-marketing companies (OMCs).  The expectation, of course, is that restricting trading in derivatives or increasing its cost will reduce speculation and take some stress off the rupee, which has been under pressure. However, these are at best stopgap measures and will not address the underlying problem. In fact, they could hurt genuine businesses that need to hedge foreign-exchange exposure. It has been reported that banks have made representations in this regard. Further, removing the OMC demand may reduce pressure in the foreign-exchange market, but it will not reduce their requirement for foreign currencies in any way. The relief in the currency market, therefore, is likely to be short-lived.  In fact, the RBI is intervening significantly in the currency market to support the rupee. The concessional swap arrangements, including for the Foreign-Currency Non-Resident (Bank) — or FCNR (B) — deposits helped accumulate foreign-exchange reserves, which increased to a record high of $785.7 billion in the week ended September 4. However, it has since declined by over $51 billion (October 2). Part of it could be on account of revaluation, but it does indicate that the central bank is fairly active in the currency market. The stated policy of the RBI is that it does not target any level and intervenes only to contain excess volatility. However, it seems to be looking at the other objectives as well.  It is worth highlighting that dealing with balance of payments (BoP) pressure is not the central bank’s responsibility alone. India is facing pressure on both the current and capital accounts, and the strain predates the war in West Asia. India faced BoP deficits over the past two years, partly because of capital outflows. This year will likely show a surplus because of strong inflows under FCNR (B). Again, FCNR (B) flows will give only short-term relief. The RBI’s recent action suggests that it is not helping even to the extent many had anticipated. Continued defence would only raise the incremental cost of pursuing this path. The textbook response to a situation like this is to allow the rupee to depreciate. However, it will help fundamentally correct the situation if Indian exporters are able to take advantage of a weak currency. For that to happen, the government needs to bring in reforms, including on tariffs. Further, the government needs to put in place conditions to attract foreign direct investment. It has been reported that the government is reviewing the framework for the bilateral investment treaty, but little is known in this regard. The present situation is a good opportunity to implement trade and investment reforms, which will provide much-needed stability on the external front and support higher growth over the medium to long term.   Topics : BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment Rupee-dollar swap Rupee vs dollar BALANCE OF PAYMENTS

entry.title: From enforcement to trust
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Editorial / From enforcement to trustFrom enforcement to trust

After process reforms, GST needs road map to shed exclusions

premium

The broader unfinished agenda for GST’s full benefits to accrue to the economy is the inclusion of items such as petrol, diesel, electricity and natural gas that remain outside its ambit

Business Standard Editorial Comment4 min read Last Updated : Oct 11 2026 | 10:44 PM ISTWhen India rolled out goods and services tax (GST) on July 1, 2017, there was a concern that the bureaucracy grappled with — the uncertainty about the revenue trajectory and the need to compensate the states for any revenue shortfall in the first five years of the new tax. One source of revenue was proceeds of the GST compensation cess levied on items such as automobiles and tobacco. The other way to address the revenue risk was to have enough checks to prevent evasion. The tax system, thus, remained geared to ensure compliance, but at the expense of procedural simplicity. But officials’ worry about revenue collection and unmanageable compensation requirement did turn out to be true when the first Covid-19 wave hit India, and GST revenues plummeted in April 2020.  Monthly gross GST receipts of the central and state governments, which averaged ₹95,515 crore in 2018-19 and ₹96,605 crore in 2019-20, fell to ₹32,172 crore in April 2020. Consequently, the central government had to borrow ₹2.69 trillion from the market to compensate the states for their revenue shortfall. The full repayment of that in 2025-26 offered the GST Council an opportunity in September last year to review the tax slabs and rates, phase out the cess, and offer a consumption stimulus by lowering the indirect tax on a range of daily use as well as aspirational items, ranging from toothpaste and shampoo to consumer electronics and cars in the biggest overhaul of the system. Also, the number of slabs was brought down to broadly two, 5 and 18 per cent, from the earlier four—5, 12, 18 and 28 per cent with cess. That helped to boost consumption demand. Private final consumption expenditure expanded 7.1 per cent in the March quarter of 2025-26 as compared to 5.6 per cent at the same time a year earlier.  The next logical step for reform obviously was cutting red tape and making life simpler for businesses. The tech-enabled tax system, which captures a large amount of data from multiple sources, has made it possible for the authorities to spot sources of revenue leakage. The GST Council’s decisions last week — to drop the arrest provision, lower the penalty from ₹25,000 to ₹10,000, recall notices issued for amounts below ₹10,000 and not to issue such notices in future, offer credits for taxes paid on input services from November and on capital goods from April next year, and simplify the norms for GST registration and refunds — are a major structural overhaul of the tax system. The prosecution threshold is also being raised from ₹1 crore to  ₹5 crore. These measures mark the transformation from a framework designed to deal with tax evasion by a few to one that facilitates honest tax payers based on trust.  However, the task is not over. Two proposals, one meant to offer annual return filing and quarterly tax payments to consumer-facing businesses with sales up to ₹5 crore and a second proposal to further ease input tax credit availability, are sought to be implemented from April next year after another round of deliberation. The broader unfinished agenda for GST’s full benefits to accrue to the economy is the inclusion of items such as petrol, diesel, electricity and natural gas that remain outside its ambit. If the tax rates are indeed going to be reviewed only once a year from hereon, that should free up the Council’s bandwidth to discuss and lay out a road map for such excluded items so that efficiencies and competitiveness are enhanced across the value chain and GST truly becomes “good and simple”.   Topics : GST goods and service tax GST Council cgst GST Act BS Opinion Business Standard Editorial Comment

From the IMF's global growth forecast and Navi Pillay's Nobel Peace Prize to India's climate needs, rising healthcare costs and the debate over welfare, today's opinions examine multiple challenges

Despite warnings of a meltdown, Trump’s policies have barely dented global growth forecasts. (Illustration: Ajaya Mohanty)

Tanmaya Nanda New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 14 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTHello and welcome to Best of Business Standard Opinion, our wrap of the day's editorial page.  The IMF’s October World Economic Outlook projects global growth at 3.1 per cent in 2026 and 3.4 per cent in 2027, while raising India’s growth forecast for the current year to 7 per cent on resilient domestic demand. Today's first editorial highlights how energy supply rerouting, inventory drawdowns, renewables and investment in artificial intelligence have helped the world economy withstand recent shocks. However, these buffers have limits, and disappointing AI returns could unsettle financial markets. Growth is also concentrating in fewer countries, heightening risks amid elevated public debt and tight financial conditions. India’s exposure to energy disruptions and limited participation in the AI boom demand policy agility.  Navi Pillay’s Nobel Peace Prize comes at a time of intensifying conflict and mounting challenges to the universality of human rights. Her choice for the Peace Nobel, notes our second editorial, delivers a restorative to the primacy of human rights in the global discourse, given that the South African jurist’s career has spanned the fight against apartheid, the prosecution of atrocities in Rwanda and efforts to advance gender justice and combat caste discrimination. Her work has also helped establish that rape and sexual assault could constitute acts of genocide. More recently, she chaired the UN commission that accused Israel of genocide in Gaza.  Nitin Desai argues that climate policy must shift beyond mitigation to prepare for unavoidable temperature rises, as countries’ emissions targets remain inadequate to meet the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C goal. With the threshold likely to be breached within years, India must integrate climate management into development planning, prioritising local adaptation to extreme heat, water stress and health risks. Desai proposes a National Climate Management Body bringing together the Centre, states and major cities to coordinate mitigation, resilience and compliance. He also calls for predictable climate finance, greater use of satellite imagery and AI, investment in carbon capture, and renewed international cooperation on technology and funding. India’s latest National Sample Survey reveals rising reported morbidity, continued dependence on private health care and stark disparities in treatment costs. The share of people reporting ailments nearly doubled in rural areas between 2017-18 and 2025, while private providers treated most non-hospitalised ailments, despite charging several times more than public facilities. Hospitalisation costs widen this financial burden, risking a medical poverty trap for vulnerable households. Vachaspati Shukla and Santosh Kumar Dash argue that expanding health insurance alone cannot ensure effective financial protection without accessible, reliable public facilities. They call for stronger primary care, district hospitals and service delivery so illness does not threaten household economic security. Neha Bhatt reviews Reetika Khera’s Freebies or Rights: Understanding Social Policy in India, which challenges the portrayal of welfare schemes as political hand-outs rather than fundamental rights. Drawing on field research and data, Khera examines programmes spanning food security, nutrition, healthcare and employment, questioning their funding, implementation and technological interventions. She warns that spending can serve corporate and philanthropic interests, while gaps in reliable data weaken accountability. Odisha, Tamil Nadu and Himachal Pradesh offer lessons in effective delivery, from nutrition and pensions to school meals and public canteens. The book makes a compelling case for treating social protection as a foundation of equality and opportunity.
