entry.title: Best of Opinion: Disruption can't be stopped; resilience lies in response
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Best of Opinion: Disruption can't be stopped; resilience lies in responseBest of Opinion: Disruption can't be stopped; resilience lies in response

The real test of a system is not whether it can prevent every disruption. It is whether it has enough buffers, flexibility and institutional capacity

Reetesh Anand3 min read Last Updated : Oct 13 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTShocks are inevitable. Currencies come under pressure, economies are hit by unexpected disturbances, companies fail, financial vulnerabilities accumulate, and geopolitical orders fragment. The real test of a system is not whether it can prevent every disruption. It is whether it has enough buffers, flexibility and institutional capacity to absorb the blow without turning stress into breakdown. Our first editorial today, “Defending the rupee”, looks at India’s response to balance-of-payments pressure and a weakening currency. The RBI has several tools, including forex reserves and measures to influence liquidity and capital flows. These can reduce volatility and help prevent disorderly market movements. But they are ultimately shock absorbers, not substitutes for stronger fundamentals. Lasting external stability will depend on better export performance, more durable capital inflows and a current account that can withstand global turbulence.  The second editorial, “A Nobel for shocks”, takes the idea into macroeconomics. The Nobel-recognised work discussed in the editorial helped economists understand how unexpected disturbances travel through economies and why some shocks fade quickly while others produce prolonged effects. Frictions in labour, prices, finance and expectations can amplify disturbances, while policy can either cushion or worsen them. The lesson is not that economies can be made shock-proof, but that understanding transmission matters enormously when disruption arrives. M S Sahoo and Sanjeev Pandey’s column, “Maximising value, not the haircut”, applies the logic to insolvency. Corporate failure is itself a shock, but the IBC should not be judged only by the gap between creditors’ original claims and eventual recoveries. Once a company is distressed, much of its value may already have been destroyed. The more meaningful question is whether the resolution process preserves and maximises what remains, keeps viable assets productive and reallocates resources efficiently. The purpose of insolvency is not to pretend the loss never happened, but to prevent further destruction. Anoop Singh’s column, “Are financial risks now building?”, turns to the financial system as a whole. Stretched valuations, non-bank finance, fiscal pressures, technological change and geopolitical uncertainty can interact in ways that are difficult to predict. The challenge for policymakers is to identify vulnerabilities early, maintain adequate buffers and ensure risks do not migrate unnoticed across markets and institutions. Financial stability depends on resilience before the shock, not improvisation after it. “Middle powers’ unconvincing new statecraft”, Talmiz Ahmad’s review of Workarounding, edited by Maximilian Mayer, Gedaliah Afterman, Narayanappa Janardhan & Laura Mahrenbach, looks at geopolitics. As the international order becomes more fragmented, middle powers are experimenting with new coalitions and workarounds. But whether these arrangements can genuinely absorb geopolitical pressure or provide strategic room remains uncertain. Disruption cannot always be stopped, show these pieces. Resilience lies in what happens next.

entry.title: Best of Opinion: Feedback ignored may return as friction, mistrust, failure
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Specials / Best of Opinion: Feedback ignored may return as friction, mistrust, failureBest of Opinion: Feedback ignored may return as friction, mistrust, failure

Healthy systems do not just impose, regulate or command. They also listen, learn and adjust before feedback becomes breakdown

Reetesh Anand New Delhi 3 min read Last Updated : Oct 12 2026 | 6:15 AM ISTStrong systems do not just act but also listen. Tax authorities need to hear what compliance feels like for businesses. Election bodies need to respond to questions about credibility. Electricity markets need to absorb the signal sent by falling renewable costs. Infrastructure planning needs to respect what mountains and rivers are telling us. Democracies, too, weaken when competing sides stop hearing each other. The common lesson across all these issues is that feedback ignored eventually returns as friction, mistrust or failure. Our first editorial today, “From enforcement to trust”, looks at the GST regime after years of aggressive action against evasion and fraud. Enforcement was necessary, but the next stage cannot be built on permanent suspicion. Businesses need simpler procedures, predictable rules, fewer intrusive interventions and a system where compliant taxpayers are not treated as potential offenders by default. The editorial argues for a shift from enforcement-heavy administration towards trust-based compliance. Tax reform matures when the state learns from how the system actually works for those inside it.  The second editorial, “A democratic debate”, turns to the Election Commission of India. Questions about electoral processes should not automatically be treated as attacks on the institution. Credibility is strengthened when concerns are answered, data is disclosed and scrutiny is taken seriously. Democratic institutions do not protect themselves by closing off debate; they strengthen themselves by engaging with it. Ajay Shah’s column, “Consequences of cheap electricity”, looks at the signal sent by falling renewable-energy costs. If clean electricity becomes substantially cheaper, it can reshape industrial location, production costs and competitiveness. But India will benefit only if power markets, transmission, regulation and pricing allow firms to respond to that signal. Cheap power is not just an energy story. It could alter the economic geography of manufacturing, but only if the institutional machinery is flexible enough to let prices guide investment. Sunita Narain’s column, “Himalayan blunders and beyond”, deals with a more physical form of feedback. Repeated landslides, floods and ecological damage in the Himalayas are warnings about the consequences of construction that ignores hydrology, geology and carrying capacity. The problem is not that the mountains have failed to warn us. It is that development repeatedly proceeds as though those warnings could be negotiated away. Better planning requires treating ecological signals as hard constraints, not inconveniences. “When culture wars killed democracy”, Hugh Eakin’s review of Victor Sebestyen’s Weimar Germany, looks back at history. The Weimar Germany experience shows how democratic systems could unravel when political disagreement turns into cultural warfare and rival camps stop recognising each other as legitimate participants. Healthy systems do not just impose, regulate or command. They also listen, learn and adjust before feedback becomes breakdown.

entry.title: A look at insurance sector reforms
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / A look at insurance sector reformsA look at insurance sector reforms

What electronic trading exchanges and central depositories did for capital markets in 1996, and credit bureaus did retail banking in 2000s, Bima Sugam and PIR are set to do for the insurance turf now

premium

Illustration: Binay Sinha

Tamal Bandyopadhyay10 min read Last Updated : Oct 11 2026 | 1:32 PM ISTRarely does an industry push back so intensely against the vision of its own regulator. That’s what we are witnessing with the insurance sector’s sharp reaction to the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India’s (Irdai) latest distribution reforms proposals.  The Insurance Brokers Association of India (IBAI) -- the apex body representing the country’s 798 licensed insurance brokers -- has expressed grave concern over the Irdai’s consultation paper, Recalibrating Economics of Insurance Distribution.  The association fears that implementing these rigid product- and channel-specific commission sub-caps, paired with a one-third reduction in insurers’ operational expense limits, put at least one million livelihoods at risk over the next five years. This aggressive tightening will ultimately end up harming policyholders.  The association believes that the structural reforms introduced in 2023 were robust enough to achieve the national goal of “Insurance for All by 2047”.  In April 2023, the Irdai had replaced rigid, product-by-product commission caps with a unified blanket limit on expenses of management (EoM). This granted complete boardroom freedom to insurance companies to design their own incentive structures for agents and intermediaries, provided the total expenses stayed within the statutory ceiling – 30 per cent of gross written premium for general insurers, 35 per cent for standalone health insurers and life insurers – based on different percentages for product line categories rather than a single overall limit.  While some institutional voices support the change, foreign investors remain anxious. One investor notes that while steps to contain mis-selling and curb excesses are welcome, the regulator appears to be disproportionately focussed on digital market intermediaries that were instrumental in building India’s pure term and health insurance markets.  A banker says the regulator is set to throw the baby out with the bathwater in its efforts to curb mis-selling, adding that nowhere in the world insurance is “bought” – it is always “sold” – and frequent regulatory “churn” in a nascent sector creates perpetual regulatory uncertainty.   What drove the regulator to intervene after the 2023 deregulation? Let the data speak. Following the removal of individual commission caps, the Motor Insurance premiums sourced by brokers grew by about 34 per cent, but distributor commissions skyrocketed by 259 per cent. The overall average motor commission settled at 24 per cent, with individual company average payouts spiking ranging between 13 and 50 per cent.  The retail health premiums from brokers grew by 53 per cent, while commissions surged by 118 per cent.  Distribution costs are rising exponentially faster than underlying premiums – a classic case of value leaking away from the policyholders.  Here are my own two bits on the matter. We must first look at how reliant India’s banking sector has become on insurance distribution to pad its bottomline. In FY26, insurance income accounted for a staggering 75.6 per cent of profit before tax for IndusInd Bank Ltd, followed by Bandhan Bank Ltd (30.8 per cent), DCB Bank Ltd (21 percent), and Yes Bank (19.3 per cent). Among the large banks, for State Bank of India it is 2.6 per cent and ICICI Bank 0.6 per cent.  Of course, the share of insurance income in a bank’s profit matrix depends on the size of the profit base; if the underlying profit is small, the percentage will look artificially high. It behaves much like bad assets -- in absolute terms, a bank’s non-performing assets might be low, but if its overall profitability is compressed, the ratio swells.  This brings us to cost efficiency, which is central to product-affordability and sustainable market growth. Higher customer acquisition costs directly penalise policyholder value and drain capital efficiency. Let us benchmark India’s cost architecture against three major Asian peers: Japan, South Korea, and China.  While direct cross-border comparisons are somewhat limited due to differing accounting standards, publicly available metrics show that life insurance acquisition costs as a percentage of total premiums are the highest in India, sitting at 12-16 per cent. In stark contrast, the comparable figure in China is 7-11 per cent, South Korea 8-12 per cent, while Japan boasts the highest efficiency at just 5-8 per cent.  Why does India lag so heavily in cost efficiency? The blame lies within our two dominant distribution pipelines: The traditional agency force and the bancassurance network.  The agency channel remains plagued by mass recruitment and expensive training cycles that yield low per-capita performance and high agent turnover. Meanwhile, under the current open architecture rules, banks are permitted to sell policies for up to nine insurers each across the life, general, and health sectors. Many of them merrily use this leverage to bundle high-margin insurance products with routine loan approvals.  An industry-wide focus on front-loaded, high first-year commissions juxtaposed against low renewal commissions forces distributors to prioritise fresh sales over long-term customer care.  Compounding the problem is a severe lack of consumer transparency. The average customer has no clue how much commission their broker or agent is pocketing. ("customer" and "their" okay? or customers?) One simple fix would be to mandate printing the exact commission amount boldly on the face of the policy document. After all, shouldn’t a client know exactly how much they are paying the intermediary they appointed? A broker’s strict customer-facing obligation should strengthen the argument for a transparent, value-linked remuneration model, rather than justifying immunity from disclosure.  Ideally, a customer should be able to choose an intermediary independently, relying on meaningful disclosures to compare one competitor against another. But in a milieu where the buyer has zero visibility regarding a broker’s past performance, regulatory penalties, or market conduct, making an informed choice is impossible. Selecting an intermediary is not the same as choosing a product: Without disclosure, the intermediary’s recommendation can easily be driven by the size of the payout rather than the actual needs of the consumer.  This inherent information asymmetry means customers rarely get to evaluate product pricing, historical claims ratios, or true suitability. Will the reintroduction of commission caps hurt the policyholder? Far from it—unchecked distribution costs are already spoling the party for the customers. In several key channels, distribution costs have grown much quicker than the underlying business, without a shred of evidence pointing to improved customer care.  Between FY23 and FY25, for Life Corporate Agents, new business premiums grew by 28 per cent, but distributor remuneration rose by 125 per cent, taking payouts to nearly 27 per cent of the first-year premium. This was frequently fattened by hidden rewards and volume incentives, adding another 30 to 60 per cent over the base commission.  Broker-sourced premiums for general insurance grew by 37 per cent, yet total commissions spiked by 173 per cent, effectively doubling the average commission rate. Motor commissions nearly tripled.  Are these soaring profits and remuneration packages truly proportionate to the effort expended, the complexity of the risk, and the ultimate value delivered to the policyholder?  The proposed framework seeks to resolve these anomalies. It plans to systematically link remuneration to actual effort and complexity, cleanly differentiate between open and closed distribution architectures, eliminate unnecessary intermediary layers, and capture all forms of alternative payouts to prevent circumvention. Group credit life payouts currently hover at around 45 per cent, while commissions for niche lines—like school buses, where the claims ratio is under 30 per cent—remain artificially high.  The high-cost distribution concentrated in existing channels has failed the consumer. It is pushing the industry to migrate towards a lower-cost, technology-driven ecosystem. The Irdai is positioning Bima Sugam and the Public Insurance Registry (PIR) as core digital public market infrastructure institutions designed to deepen market penetration.  Bima Sugam – collectively owned by 58 insurance companies and managed by the Bima Sugam India Federation – is set to roll out its initial motor insurance marketplace in November 2026. By January 2027, the platform will expand to include retail health products, followed sequentially by pure term-life policies.  Meanwhile, the PIR is being built to function for the insurance sector exactly how the Unified Payments Interface (UPI) revolutionised digital banking. Rather than acting as a rigid, centralised repository, it operates as an interoperable information exchange layer that securely connects life, health, and motor data across all underwriting platforms.  Once fully operational, PIR will eliminate the friction of app-hopping. Policyholders will be able to track upcoming renewals, verify critical nominee details, and update contact or banking credentials across multiple distinct insurers simultaneously. Transparency will make it vastly easier for families to discover dormant or unclaimed insurance payouts. Insurers, too, stand to benefit from this digital architecture through more robust risk assessment, advanced fraud detection, and the seamless porting of health policies between competing providers.  In a structural sense, what electronic trading exchanges and central depositories did for the capital markets in 1996, and what credit bureaus did for retail banking in the early 2000s, Bima Sugam and PIR are primed to execute for the insurance landscape today.  However, to ensure this transition succeeds without breaking the industry’s backbone, the regulator must balance its enthusiasm with operational reality. Along with slashing distributor commissions, the Irdai’s proposal to aggressively cap corporate operational expenses by tightening individual EoM limits requires careful calibration.  As an insurance company’s baseline cost of operations is inherently tied to the size and maturity of its balance sheet, squeezing acquisition costs and corporate overhead simultaneously could choke growth. Even with the proposed five-year glide path starting in FY28, the regulator would be wise to re-examine the systemic risks of tightening both levers simultaneously.  To offset the inevitable drop in distributor income and prevent a mass exodus of talent, the regulatory framework should actively look to expand the commercial scope of traditional intermediaries. Insurance distributors should be permitted to sell basic capital market products after undergoing structured, certified cross-training.  Simultaneously, why shouldn’t commercial banks be allowed to scale up their risk advisory capabilities? While independent insurance brokers operate with no policy sum insured limits, banks face strict, capped limits despite being licensed corporate agents for selling insurance. Equalising these rules would allow banks to leverage their massive institutional muscle to build capabilities and offer comprehensive risk management.  The Irdai has already taken a progressive step by proposing slashing of the minimum capital requirement for establishing an insurance brokerage from ₹75 lakh down to ₹10 lakh. This capital reduction will act as a major catalyst, incentivising smaller brokers to set up shop in tier-2 and tier-3 towns. To complement this grassroots push, the regulator should formalise a framework, allowing rural business correspondents to market standardised insurance policies.  Finally, India boasts a massive network of 527,488 common services centres set up under the Digital India initiative to deliver electronic public utilities, financial services, and healthcare access to rural citizens. If these micro-entrepreneurs are systematically trained and licensed to distribute basic insurance products, they can be transformed into an instant, nationwide grassroots workforce.  We must welcome structural distribution reforms if we are to clear the path for the national dream of achieving “Insurance for All by 2047”. But for that dream to manifest, the regulator must complement its hard commission caps with progressive, multi-product revenue avenues that keep India’s vast distribution workforce financially viable.  ____________________________________________________________________________________________________ The writer is an author and senior advisor to Jana Small Finance Bank Ltd. His latest book: Roller Coaster: An Affair with Banking. To read his previous columns, log on to www.bankerstrust.in. X: @TamalBandyo        Disclaimer: These are personal views of the writer. entry.title: Modi at 25: Small signs, big challenge
entry.content:
Home / Opinion / Columns / Modi at 25: Small signs, big challengeModi at 25: Small signs, big challenge

Multiple headwinds make the turbulence Mr Modi is battling as he steps into his 26th year in public office. This has brought the three-point Modi proposition under the greatest pressure since 2014

Prime Minister Narendra Modi (Image: Bloomberg)

Shekhar Gupta7 min read Last Updated : Oct 10 2026 | 9:30 AM ISTThis is the season of looking at Narendra Modi’s 25 years in power and beyond. His followers are celebrating. His Cabinet has passed a resolution praising him. Of course, the critics are out dissecting his quarter-century in public life, not with a scalpel but with a scythe. It’s also the season for people, especially journalists, telling their “when I first met Modi” stories. I’ll hold on to mine for another day. Let’s not risk diluting today’s serious argument. Two weeks ago, we noted that for any incumbent in India, the third year of a term is the toughest. This is when challenges build up, fatigue sets in, aspiring successors sharpen the knives. We also said that the last of these doesn’t apply to Mr Modi. Nobody in his party would even dare to whisper the “S” word.  The third year of Mr Modi’s third term, however, is beset with all of the other challenges. His tired and incomplete Cabinet is struggling. His chief ministers — barring Yogi Adityanath, Devendra Fadnavis and Himanta Biswa Sarma — aren’t up to the multiple challenges. Having used the ancient editorial privilege of ‘tabooing’ a word, and listing the cliched “narrative” under it, I then can’t use it. The fact is, this market of popular opinion is rife with competing, contradictory notions. The Modi-BJP story is still the most significant. It just isn’t as dominant as before. Multiple breezes make the turbulence Mr Modi is battling as he steps into his 26th year in public office. 

Also Read

Jaishankar holds talks with Ethiopian counterpart; discusses trade

Back to the future: Can Kolkata's iconic trams make a grand comeback?premium

Ruling parties sweep bypolls in Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, Assam, Puducherry

When the crops wiltpremium

This has brought the classical — and so far all-conquering — three-point Modi proposition under the greatest pressure since 2014. The three points are: Hard, Hinduised nationalism; ever-expanding welfare, distributed efficiently, with minimal friction or leakage; and visible construction of physical infrastructure. All of this without significant overhang of corruption. The Modi proposition survives. It’s just that several other factors have now emerged. And we aren’t just talking about the rebellion of an irreverential, ageist, educated and mostly not-impoverished GenZ.  What makes this period of crisis unprecedented in Mr Modi’s prime ministership is the convergence of these factors.. Like the Shakespearean “when sorrows come, they come not single spies, but in battalions.” In isolation, each of these factors may look small. But they become formidable when the big picture comes together. As the great management guru late C K Prahalad used to say: “Weak signals add up to a big change.” He elaborated this in his oft-quoted 1995 paper “Weak Signals Versus Strong Paradigms” (Sage Journals). Prahalad himself summarised it thus: “Taken one at a time, these signals don’t add up to much. But taken together, they present a picture of a country (or industry) in dramatic transformation.” Is this what Mr Modi is confronted with now? Let’s check out some facts. I am reducing these “battalions of sorrows” to a dozen most significant. 1. Dramatic damage to the credibility of the Election Commission of India (ECI), and thereby growing doubts over the integrity of the election process. 2. A growing belief that the top judiciary either doesn’t dare look the executive in the eye, or gives wishy-washy orders. Worse, that it speaks with a forked tongue. Ironically, this view is shared on both sides. 3. A solitary retired civil servant (Subhash Chandra Garg) has triggered a nationwide debate on the credibility of gross domestic product figures. 4. Inflation, as now forecast by the RBI, is set to rise to its highest level in nearly three years, and the rupee is struggling despite a highly successful, if expensive, dollar-deposit scheme. 5. Two of this establishment’s most trusted civil servants, the two Election Commissioners (ECs), protected their own backs by creating a paper trail to record their opposition to the Chief Election Commissioner’s decisions. 6. Ability of the Opposition, especially Rahul Gandhi, to lay siege to the Capital with English TV channels and Hindi newspapers, including the ones ‘most trusted’ by the establishment, giving it prominent airtime. 7. Young people lampooning the Prime Minister with mere feckless pushback from his “Right-wing” supporters, and an overnight phenomenon like CJP setting the agenda, from Neet to the state of government schools. 8. A small ally like Chirag Paswan taking a swipe at Bihar government over law and order. And a way smaller ally, Om Prakash Rajbhar, going public with his purported conversation with the Prime Minister on Uttar Pradesh’s division into multiple states, which Yogi Adityanath firmly opposes. 9. Contrary to the Modi government’s decisive image, we’ve seen festering indecisiveness —whether to press ahead with delimitation, or what to do with a Parliament session that has not been prorogued even two months after its adjournment sine die. To the naked eye, it shows a lack of confidence in marshalling the numbers for constitutional amendments the BJP really wants.  10. Inability, one can also add prolonged hesitation in carrying out a Cabinet reshuffle, or at least filling the vacant slots. There are too many of them, including education. 11. Continued value destruction in the stock market across Mr Modi’s third term, even as all global peers, from the US and Europe to Japan, South Korea, China and even Pakistan, have boomed. The disinclination to acknowledge the challenge is a self-destructive cop-out when millions from the middle class have moved their savings into systematic investment plans and are celebrated by the government for doing so. It also amounts to them having given the fleeing foreign portfolio investors (FPI), a golden handshake. 12. And finally, a global situation for India not seen in decades. Donald Trump has narrowed India’s strategic space in many areas. He’s also challenging our claims to strategic autonomy, with a provocation a day. Beyond Mr Trump, the war in Ukraine, smouldering West Asia, roiled energy markets, and a newly opened strategic-rentier window for Pakistan. All of these have come on top of a deficient monsoon. That’s beyond any government’s control. But these simmering discontents will play out in a below-average farming year. The larger issues, however, are rooted in the three most fundamental factors that have made India cohesive, and stronger over the decades. These are trust in the Constitution and the belief that nobody can take it away, fairness of the top judiciary, and independence of the Election Commission. All three are under strain now. The BJP knows better than its opponents how badly it was damaged in 2024 by rumours fed by just the odd statement from its middling functionaries and the Ayodhya candidate that the party needed 400 seats to change the Constitution. Now most Indians have not read the Constitution, or even the 106 amendments already carried out. But they see the Constitution almost like a deity or a scripture. Fair, secular, a bill of rights they won’t let anybody take away. Constant talk of special Parliament sessions have brought back these suspicions. The Supreme Court has unfortunately built a well-deserved reputation of flip-flops, cynical prevarications, and talking more than writing. This also applies to its treatment of the SIR issue so far. It’s being watched closely now as it battles multiple challenges—from restoring the credibility of the ECI to taking a view on the right to protest in the Capital. And finally, the ECI. Through nearly eight decades, the institution has had good days and bad, and some indifferent ones. It was, however, never as broken as it is now. An ECI caught in an every-man-for-himself trap will struggle to win back popular confidence. It’s a national crisis. These are the challenges Mr Modi needs to address as he steps into his 26th unbroken year in public office. If he doesn’t, or fails to do so, C.K. Prahalad’s small signals could lead to a dramatic crisis over a very painful two and a half years until the summer of 2029.
